content.title: Continuity and the Intermediate Value Theorem
content.overview: This lesson focuses on the formal definition of continuity at a point and the application of the Intermediate Value Theorem (IVT) to guarantee the existence of specific function values on a closed interval.
learning_objectives: Define continuity at a point using limits and function values.
Verify continuity on a closed interval [a, b].
Apply the Intermediate Value Theorem to justify the existence of a value c such that f(c) = k.

sections.title: The Three-Part Definition of Continuity
sections.content:
For a function f(x) to be continuous at a point x = a, three conditions must be met: 1. f(a) must be defined (the point exists). 2. The limit of f(x) as x approaches a must exist (the left-hand and right-hand limits are equal). 3. The limit of f(x) as x approaches a must equal the function value f(a). If any of these fail, the function is discontinuous at that point.

![A sequence of steps to justify continuity at a point: check if f(a) is defined, check if the limit exists, and check if the limit equals f(a).](https://img.justsolvely.com/followUpImage/cdc6335d-028c-4f13-90cf-313a262e07c6-1786519334391-969.webp)

sections.title: The Intermediate Value Theorem (IVT)
sections.content: The IVT states that if a function f is continuous on a closed interval [a, b], then for every value k between f(a) and f(b), there exists at least one value c in the open interval (a, b) such that f(c) = k. This theorem is an 'existence theorem'; it guarantees that a value exists but does not necessarily provide a formula to find it.

sections.title: Justification Requirements
sections.content: To use the IVT in a formal justification, you must explicitly state that the function is continuous on the specific closed interval. You must also show the calculation of the endpoint values f(a) and f(b) and demonstrate that the target value k lies between them (e.g., f(a) < k < f(b)).

worked_examples.question: Let g(x) be defined as g(x) = (x^2 - 9)/(x - 3) for x ≠ 3 and g(3) = 6. Justify that g(x) is continuous at x = 3 and use the IVT to show there is a c in [3, 5] such that g(c) = 7.
worked_examples.solution: Step 1: Check continuity at x = 3. The value g(3) = 6 is defined. The limit as x approaches 3 of (x^2 - 9)/(x - 3) is the limit of (x-3)(x+3)/(x-3), which is the limit of (x+3) as x approaches 3, equaling 6. Since the limit (6) equals the value g(3) (6), g is continuous at x = 3. Step 2: Check the interval [3, 5]. Since g(x) simplifies to x + 3 for all x, it is continuous everywhere. Step 3: Evaluate endpoints. g(3) = 6 and g(5) = 5 + 3 = 8. Step 4: Apply IVT. Since g is continuous on [3, 5] and 6 < 7 < 8, the IVT guarantees a c in (3, 5) such that g(c) = 7. (Solving x + 3 = 7 gives c = 4, which is in the interval).

common_mistakes: Applying IVT to a function that has a jump or vertical asymptote within the interval.
Failing to explicitly state that the function is continuous before citing IVT.
Attempting to use IVT when the target value k is outside the range of the endpoint values f(a) and f(b).
Confusing the existence of a limit with the existence of continuity (forgetting to check if the limit equals the function value).
exam_tips: Always write 'Since f is continuous on [a, b]...' as your first sentence in an IVT justification.
Show the inequality f(a) < k < f(b) or f(b) < k < f(a) clearly to prove the target value is bracketed.
If a function is a polynomial, rational, power, or trigonometric function, state it is continuous on its domain as part of your justification.
content.recap: Continuity at a point requires the limit to exist and equal the function value. If a function is continuous on [a, b], the IVT guarantees that all y-values between f(a) and f(b) are attained at least once by some x-value c in the interval.

knowledge_claims.content: Continuity at a point x = a requires that f(a) is defined, the limit as x approaches a exists, and the limit equals f(a).
A function is continuous on a closed interval [a, b] if it is continuous at every point in the open interval (a, b) and possesses one-sided continuity at the endpoints.
The Intermediate Value Theorem (IVT) is an existence theorem that guarantees a value c exists but does not necessarily provide the value of c.
To justify the IVT, one must first confirm and state that the function is continuous on the closed interval [a, b].
Before applying IVT, verify that the target value k lies strictly between the endpoint values f(a) and f(b).
It is a mistake to assume the IVT applies if there is a point of discontinuity, such as a hole or asymptote, anywhere between the endpoints a and b.
If the limit of f(x) as x approaches a exists but does not equal f(a), the function has a removable discontinuity at x = a.
The IVT can be used to prove the existence of roots by showing that f(a) and f(b) have opposite signs (one positive, one negative).
The formal condition for the IVT is: if f is continuous on [a, b] and f(a) < k < f(b), then there exists c in (a, b) such that f(c) = k.
Unlike the limit, which describes behavior near a point, continuity describes the behavior at the point itself by linking the limit to the actual output.
When evaluating the limit of a piecewise function at the boundary, you must check that the left-hand limit equals the right-hand limit.
If a function is continuous on [a, b], its graph can be drawn from x = a to x = b without lifting the pencil.

items.stem: Which procedure or value is mathematically consistent in “AP Calculus BC — Continuity and the Intermediate Value Theorem — Practice Record 01”?

options.A: Continuity and the Intermediate Value Theorem: Continuity at a point requires an existing limit equal to the function value, and the Intermediate Value Theorem guarantees attained values under interval continuity.
options.B: Implicit Differentiation: When variables are related implicitly, differentiating both sides with respect to the independent variable introduces derivative factors for dependent-variable terms.
options.C: Mean Value and Extreme Value Theorems: Theorems guarantee extrema or a derivative equal to an average rate only when their continuity and differentiability hypotheses are satisfied.
options.D: Numerical Integration and Error Direction: Trapezoidal and midpoint approximations use tabular data, and concavity or monotonicity can determine likely over- or underestimation.

items.explanation: Choice A is best because Continuity at a point requires an existing limit equal to the function value, and the Intermediate Value Theorem guarantees attained values under interval continuity. The other options invoke different atomic topics and do not satisfy the record's stated target as directly.

items.stem: Which relationship connects the verbal and symbolic information in “AP Calculus BC — Continuity and the Intermediate Value Theorem — Practice Record 02”?

options.A: Derivatives of Inverse Functions: The derivative of an inverse at an output is the reciprocal of the original derivative at the corresponding input when that derivative is nonzero.
options.B: Continuity and the Intermediate Value Theorem: Continuity at a point requires an existing limit equal to the function value, and the Intermediate Value Theorem guarantees attained values under interval continuity.
options.C: Increasing, Decreasing, and Critical Points: The sign of the first derivative determines intervals of increase and decrease and helps classify local extrema at critical points.
options.D: Integration by Parts and Partial Fractions: Integration by parts reverses the product rule, while partial fractions decomposes rational functions into simpler integrable terms.
